title: Is Runna's Strength Training Enough If You Lift? Runna vs Kiron — Kiron
description: Runna's strength sessions are built for runners, not lifters. When they're enough, when to add a lifting plan, and how Runna and Kiron compare on price.

jsonLd.headline: Is Runna's Strength Training Enough If You Actually Lift?
jsonLd.description: Runna's strength sessions are built for runners, not lifters. When they're enough, when to add a lifting plan, and how Runna and Kiron compare on price.

body:
We make Kiron, so weigh this accordingly. Everything here about Runna comes from its App Store listing, its help and press pages, recent App Store reviews and the independent running site the5krunner, checked November 15, 2026. Everything about Kiron describes version 1.2.

If you lift and you've started running with Runna, you've probably wondered whether its strength sessions could replace your own lifting. The short answer: they're built to make you a sturdier runner, and for that job they're fine. If you want your squat or bench to keep going up, they're thin. Runna is also the stronger running coach of the two apps here, and nothing below pretends otherwise. The real question is what to do about the lifting.

The quick answer

  • Stay with Runna alone if a race is the goal and you lift once or twice a week to stay durable. That's what its sessions are designed for.
  • Use Runna for runs and Kiron for lifting if you want Runna's pace targets and a lifting program that progresses. You pay for both: $119.99 a year for Runna plus {{kiron:price-annual}} for Kiron.
  • Use Kiron for both if you'd rather have one plan and one calendar and don't need pace targets, for {{kiron:price-annual}}. Kiron 1.2 doesn't record runs or show pace, and it has no Watch app.

Runna is the better running coach. Kiron is the better home for a lifting program. Pick by which matters more to you this season.

What Runna's strength sessions are built for

Runna, which Strava bought in 2025, is a running-plan app first. Strength is an add-on you set up under Plan, then Manage Plan, then Strength. You choose:

  • A goal. Running Focus puts the emphasis on legs and core, with minimal upper-body work. All-Round Strength balances upper and lower body.
  • A length and a number. Sessions are 30, 45 or 60 minutes, up to four a week. Runna's own guide suggests one a week to hold your strength through heavy running, two as a balanced option, and three for building strength in the off-season.
  • Your equipment. Pick from a stretch band, barbell, box, bench, dumbbells, kettlebell, pull-up bar and Swiss ball, or nothing for bodyweight sessions. Runna fits the workouts to your list.

The sessions land on your training calendar and move like runs. You log reps and weight as you go, and Runna keeps your numbers under the Exercise tab. Its help pages also spell out the limits: you can't create custom strength workouts, you can't swap an exercise in the app (you can skip it, or do a similar one on your own), progression isn't described beyond tracking your weights, and strength sessions don't sync to smartwatches, so you follow them on your phone. According to the5krunner, they're part of the paid subscription.

App Store reviewers are split. Of 500 recent US reviews (January to November 2026), 41 mention strength, lifting, weights or the gym. Of those about the strength sessions, at least 14 praise them and 10 criticize them, mostly as too light, not editable, or ignoring the equipment the reviewer had selected. One called the lifts "basically just a 45 minute warmup" (an App Store reviewer, June 2026), while a personal trainer said they'd picked up new exercises for runners from them. Both can be true: the sessions are support work for running.

Five signs you've outgrown Runna's strength sessions

  1. You want a lift to go up on a schedule. Runna records your weights, but its help pages don't describe it adding weight for you. Chasing a bigger squat means doing that arithmetic yourself.
  2. You want to pick the exercises. No custom workouts and no in-app swaps. If a movement doesn't suit you, you skip it or improvise.
  3. Your upper body matters to you. Running Focus keeps upper-body work minimal by design. All-Round Strength adds it, but the exercises are still Runna's choice.
  4. You lift longer or more often. Sessions top out at 60 minutes and four a week. If your lifting runs past an hour, or five days a week, Runna can't plan it.
  5. You already have a program. A coach's plan, a book program or a ChatGPT plan can't go into Runna. You can log a session by hand under Progress, then Activities, but Runna won't schedule it or progress it.

If two or more of these sound like you, read on. If none do, Runna's sessions are probably enough, and the third setup below is yours.

Three ways to set up the week

Each setup is good at something different: pace coaching, lifting progress, or keeping everything in one place. Each sample week follows our guide to running and lifting in the same week: keep 24 to 36 hours between your heaviest leg session and your fastest run, and keep easy days easy.

Setup 1: Runna for the runs, Kiron for the lifting

Who it's for: a lifter training for a race who wants Runna's pace targets and a lifting program that actually progresses.

In Runna, set your runs per week, running days and long-run day under Plan, then Manage Plan, then Running Schedule; the minimum is two runs a week. Skip Runna's strength setup. In Kiron, start Upper / Lower Strength, a four-day program, on its suggested days. Its sessions run in order from the day you start, so start it on a weekend or a Monday to put Lower 1 on Monday. With Runna at two runs and a Sunday long run:

  • Monday, Kiron: Lower 1, Heavy Squat. Back squat 4×4 and Romanian deadlift 3×6–8, then leg press, leg curls and calf raises.
  • Tuesday, Kiron: Upper 1, Heavy Bench and Press. Bench press 4×4, overhead press 3×5 and barbell row 4×6–8, then pulldowns and pushdowns.
  • Wednesday, Runna: a run with Runna's pace targets, two days after the heavy squats.
  • Thursday, Kiron: Lower 2, Heavy Deadlift. Deadlift 3×4 and dumbbell split squats 3×8–10 a leg, then back extensions, leg curls and calf raises.
  • Friday, Kiron: Upper 2, a lighter day of dumbbell and cable work for 8 to 15 reps.
  • Saturday: rest.
  • Sunday, Runna: the long run, three days after the deadlifts.

Kiron adds 5 lb (2.5 kg) to a heavy lift when you finish every rep of every set, or more when your last set had reps to spare. Want a third run? Add a running day in Runna; an easy run sits fine after an upper-body day.

The two apps don't talk to each other directly. What links them is Kiron's recovery map, which counts runs and rides that other apps or your watch save to Apple Health or Health Connect from the last 10 days. If your Runna runs land there, Kiron counts them, and when today's lifting leans on legs that are still tired, it says why and offers an easier session, with Undo. Check that your runs actually show up in Apple Health or Health Connect first.

Cost: Runna Premium at $119.99 a year, plus Kiron at {{kiron:price-annual}}.

Setup 2: Kiron for both

Who it's for: a lifter who runs for fitness, or for a race without a time goal, and wants one plan and one calendar.

Start Run + Lift: two full-body barbell days and two runs a week, with no end date. It suggests Monday, Wednesday, Thursday and Sunday, and runs its sessions in order on the days you pick, from the day you start; the program page shows which comes first. Started on a Monday, week one is:

  • Monday: Lift A, Squat and Bench. Squat 3×5, bench press 3×5, barbell row 3×8 and dumbbell step-ups 2×8–10 a leg.
  • Tuesday: rest.
  • Wednesday: Easy Run, 35 minutes, at a pace where you can talk.
  • Thursday: Lift B, Deadlift and Press. Deadlift 1×5, overhead press 3×5, chin-ups 3×5–8 and dumbbell Romanian deadlifts 2×8–10.
  • Friday and Saturday: rest.
  • Sunday: Long Run, 5 miles to start. The notes say to add half a mile every other week and cut back a mile every fourth week.

Training for a race? Kiron's running plans include Beginner 5K (9 weeks), Run a 10K (10 weeks), Half Marathon (12 weeks, four runs a week) and Marathon (16 weeks, five runs a week). They run in phases on their own weekdays, and the longer three end with a taper and a race week. Start one next to a lifting program, such as the Beginner 5×5 in our post on StrongLifts alternatives: Kiron asks whether to replace your current program or run both, and both share one calendar. Or paste a hybrid plan from a coach or ChatGPT under Import a plan.

How runs work in Kiron. Each run shows a time or distance target with an effort cue, such as "comfortably hard" for tempo work. Kiron doesn't record GPS or show pace in 1.2: run with your watch or phone app, then type the time and distance into the run's card. You can shorten or lengthen a run on a busy day; race days are left as they are. Kiron also needs a connection to open a workout.

Recovery. Kiron's muscle map works out effort from the weights and reps you log and, for cardio, from heart rate, with a cardio ring and training load alongside. It also counts runs and rides other apps save to Apple Health or Health Connect, so you get one picture of how tired your legs are from both. Our guide to recovery time by muscle group covers how long each muscle typically needs.

Cost: {{kiron:pricing-sentence}} Kept all year, the weekly plan comes to {{kiron:price-weekly-yearly}}, so compare yearly with yearly. Kiron is also new, where Runna has a large community behind it.

Setup 3: Runna alone, with its strength sessions

Who it's for: a runner whose goal is a race, who lifts to stay durable rather than to add weight to the bar. With three runs, a Sunday long run and two 45-minute Running Focus sessions:

  • Monday: Runna strength, Running Focus.
  • Tuesday: Runna run.
  • Wednesday: rest.
  • Thursday: Runna run.
  • Friday: Runna strength, Running Focus.
  • Saturday: rest.
  • Sunday: Runna long run.

Runna picks the run types, the paces and the strength exercises; you pick the days. Runna alone is the right call if:

  • your goal is a race time, and you want pace targets that Runna sets from your ability and recent race times, then suggests changing as you train
  • you track your runs on an Apple Watch, Garmin or COROS watch
  • one or two strength sessions a week is all the lifting you want
  • you'd use the extras: the Runna club, its events, and live yoga and pilates classes

Cost: $119.99 a year, or $149.99 a year for the Strava + Runna bundle.

Questions lifters ask about Runna

Does Runna have strength training?

Yes. You add it under Plan, then Manage Plan, then Strength, and choose Running Focus or All-Round Strength, 30 to 60 minutes a session, up to four a week. The sessions are pre-built and fitted to your equipment, and you can't create your own or swap exercises in the app.

How much is Runna?

On the US App Store, Runna Premium is $19.99 a month or $119.99 a year, checked November 15, 2026, and the Strava + Runna bundle is $149.99 a year. Without paying, you get week 1 of any plan plus run recording, according to the5krunner.

Can I use Runna with a lifting app?

Yes. For a lifter with a race on the calendar it's a sensible split: Runna plans the runs and the lifting app runs the program, as in Setup 1. If your runs reach Apple Health or Health Connect, Kiron's recovery map counts them alongside your lifting. Our guide to workout apps for following a program covers other lifting apps too.

Is Runna worth it if I mostly lift?

If you run two or three times a week without a race time in mind, you may not need a running coach at all: easy runs plus one longer run cover it, and Kiron's Run + Lift puts exactly that next to your lifting. If you're chasing a race time, Runna's pace targets are worth paying for, and your lifting can live in a separate app.

If you lift first and run second, try Kiron's Run + Lift, or start a race plan next to the lifting program you already follow. {{kiron:cta-sentence}} Get Kiron. If pace coaching for a race is what you're after, Runna is the right tool, and its first week is free.
